retirements.name: Retirements and capacity growth restrictions
facts: (top) :: As Azure continues to invest in higher-performing, more secure, and modern compute infrastructure, it moves away from older-generation hardware. Azure infrastructure expansion focuses on deploying newer-generation hardware that supports the latest virtual machine (VM) offerings.

(top) :: As a result, certain VM series in the End of Life lifecycle stage have an announced retirement date, and some are also subject to capacity growth restrictions starting in July 2026. Plan to modernize to newer-generation VM families and series to ensure continued access to current platform capabilities, improved performance, enhanced security, and long-term capacity availability.

Frequently asked questions > Are there pricing differences between End of Life and newer VM families? :: Pricing, performance, storage capabilities, and hardware characteristics might vary across VM generations. Validate workload requirements and review the documentation for the recommended target VM families and series before you modernize.
Frequently asked questions > Can a new subscription deploy an affected VM SKU? :: No. New subscriptions are restricted from deploying the affected VM series.

Frequently asked questions > Can an existing subscription continue deploying affected VM SKUs after July 31, 2026? :: Quota is an approved limit; it isn't a capacity reservation or guarantee. A VM deployment might still encounter an allocation failure if capacity is unavailable in the requested region or zone.

Frequently asked questions > Can an existing subscription continue deploying affected VM SKUs after July 31, 2026? :: Yes. An existing subscription can continue to deploy, redeploy, and operate affected VM SKUs within its already-approved quota, subject to capacity availability.

Frequently asked questions > Can an existing subscription request more quota for an affected VM series? :: No. You can't get more quota for affected VM series. Plan new growth on newer-generation VM series.

Frequently asked questions > Can customers continue normal operations on existing VMs and environments as long as they stay within their approved quota? :: Existing subscriptions with previously approved quota aren't affected by this change. Customers can continue deploying impacted VM SKUs within their existing approved quota limits, subject to capacity availability. However, approved quota doesn't guarantee capacity availability in the region and deployments might still fail if sufficient capacity isn't available.

Frequently asked questions > Does reimaging one of the impacted VM series in a Virtual Machine Scale Set deallocate it? :: No. Reimaging replaces the OS disk so that operating-system and configuration changes can be applied. It doesn't remove the VM or change its VM series. For details, see Reimage a virtual machine in a scale set.

Frequently asked questions > Does this restriction mean the D(s)v3 and E(s)v3 VM series are retired? :: No. This restriction is about capacity growth, not retirement. Retirement follows a separate process with dedicated customer communications, timelines, and transition guidance.

Frequently asked questions > Does this restriction mean the D(s)v3 and E(s)v3 VM series are retired? :: Separately from these capacity growth restrictions, the Dv3, Dsv3, Ev3, and Esv3 series are in the End of Life stage and retire on November 15, 2029. Until that date, these series remain supported under Azure SLAs, subject to the capacity growth restrictions in this article. For retirement details, see Retired and retiring VM size series.

Frequently asked questions > How do I identify the best replacement VM for my workload? :: Azure provides VM modernization guidance to help you identify the most appropriate replacement VM family and series based on workload requirements, performance needs, and storage compatibility considerations. Review the VM modernization guidance before selecting a replacement VM.

Frequently asked questions > On-demand capacity reservations (ODCR) > Can I continue deploying VMs against an existing capacity reservation for an impacted VM series? :: Yes. You can continue deploying VMs against an existing capacity reservation within the reservation's allocated capacity. You don't need extra quota to deploy VMs that consume capacity already reserved within the same subscription.

Frequently asked questions > On-demand capacity reservations (ODCR) > Can I continue deploying VMs against an existing capacity reservation for an impacted VM series? :: You might encounter problems when using shared capacity reservations across subscriptions. In this scenario, the consuming subscription might require extra quota to use the shared reservation. Because quota increases are restricted for the affected VM series, this scenario could prevent extra deployments even when reserved capacity is available.

Frequently asked questions > On-demand capacity reservations (ODCR) > Can I create new capacity reservations for impacted VM series after the quota restriction is implemented? :: Yes, as long as quota is already available within an existing subscription. However, be aware that scenarios involving shared capacity reservations across subscriptions might be impacted because you can't grant extra quota to consuming subscriptions after the quota freeze takes effect.

Frequently asked questions > On-demand capacity reservations (ODCR) > Do existing capacity reservations for impacted VM series continue to function after the quota restriction takes effect? :: Yes. Existing on-demand capacity reservations (ODCRs) continue to function because they consume existing quota allocations. You can continue using your reservations up to the limits of both your available quota and reserved capacity.

Frequently asked questions > Reserved instances > Do RIs provide protection from growth restrictions, and how do they work with on-demand capacity reservations? :: Customers who require capacity assurance should evaluate on-demand capacity reservations (ODCRs). Customers who need flexibility across VM families or regions should consider Azure Savings Plan for Compute.

Frequently asked questions > Reserved instances > Do RIs provide protection from growth restrictions, and how do they work with on-demand capacity reservations? :: Purchasing an RI doesn't reserve capacity or protect against capacity growth restrictions. RIs provide a discount for eligible usage but don't guarantee capacity availability.

Frequently asked questions > Reserved instances > Do RIs provide protection from growth restrictions, and how do they work with on-demand capacity reservations? :: RIs and ODCRs serve different purposes: RIs provide billing discounts, while ODCRs reserve capacity for a specific VM size, region, and zone.

Frequently asked questions > Reserved instances > What commitment discounts remain available, and how should I plan future purchases or renewals? :: Azure Savings Plan for Compute remains available as a flexible commitment option across eligible VM generations.

Frequently asked questions > Reserved instances > What commitment discounts remain available, and how should I plan future purchases or renewals? :: For affected applicable A, B, D, E, F, or L variants of v1 through v3 VM series, new or renewed one-year and three-year RIs are no longer available.

Frequently asked questions > Reserved instances > What commitment discounts remain available, and how should I plan future purchases or renewals? :: For newer VM generations, RIs remain available for eligible VM series.

Frequently asked questions > Reserved instances > What commitment discounts remain available, and how should I plan future purchases or renewals? :: Review the reservation portfolio before February 1, 2027, and plan how to use any remaining exchange rights for eligible active RIs. For more information, see Manage Azure Reservations.

Frequently asked questions > Reserved instances > What happens to existing RIs and costs when I modernize from applicable A, B, D, E, F, or L variants of v1 through v3 series to v5 or later? :: RI exchanges are available until February 1, 2027. After that date, each eligible active reservation purchased before the deadline retains one final exchange.

Frequently asked questions > Reserved instances > What happens to existing RIs and costs when I modernize from applicable A, B, D, E, F, or L variants of v1 through v3 series to v5 or later? :: RIs don't automatically transfer when you modernize to a different VM series. Exchange an eligible RI to match the new VM series or transition to Azure Savings Plan for Compute. If you don't make an update, the RI might no longer apply, which could result in additional costs.

Frequently asked questions > Reserved instances > What options are available for customers with large usage of applicable A, B, D, E, F, or L variants of v1 through v3 when existing RIs expire? Is there an exception process for RI renewals? :: Affected applicable A, B, D, E, F, or L variants of v1 through v3 RIs can't be renewed or repurchased after expiration. Once expired, usage moves to pay-as-you-go rates unless you select another commitment option.

Frequently asked questions > Reserved instances > What options are available for customers with large usage of applicable A, B, D, E, F, or L variants of v1 through v3 when existing RIs expire? Is there an exception process for RI renewals? :: Continue running affected VMs at pay-as-you-go rates.

Frequently asked questions > Reserved instances > What options are available for customers with large usage of applicable A, B, D, E, F, or L variants of v1 through v3 when existing RIs expire? Is there an exception process for RI renewals? :: Existing RIs remain valid through their committed term and continue providing discounts for eligible usage. However, no exceptions or extensions are planned for RI purchase or renewal end dates. Work with your Microsoft account team to evaluate modernization and alternative commitment options.

Frequently asked questions > Reserved instances > What options are available for customers with large usage of applicable A, B, D, E, F, or L variants of v1 through v3 when existing RIs expire? Is there an exception process for RI renewals? :: Modernize to newer VM generations and purchase new RIs, an Azure Savings Plan for Compute, or both.

Frequently asked questions > Reserved instances > What options are available for customers with large usage of applicable A, B, D, E, F, or L variants of v1 through v3 when existing RIs expire? Is there an exception process for RI renewals? :: Transition to Azure Savings Plan for Compute.

Frequently asked questions > Reserved instances > What options are available for customers with large usage of applicable A, B, D, E, F, or L variants of v1 through v3 when existing RIs expire? Is there an exception process for RI renewals? :: You can:

Frequently asked questions > Reserved instances > Will existing reserved instances (RIs) continue to work after the quota growth restrictions, including during redeployment, disaster recovery, or failover? :: Existing subscriptions can deploy or redeploy affected VM sizes within approved quota, subject to capacity availability. New subscriptions, additional quota, and capacity expansion might be restricted.

Frequently asked questions > Reserved instances > Will existing reserved instances (RIs) continue to work after the quota growth restrictions, including during redeployment, disaster recovery, or failover? :: RIs are billing benefits, not capacity reservations. An RI discount might apply to matching usage, but it doesn't guarantee VM creation, redeployment, disaster recovery, failover, or scaling if capacity is unavailable.

Frequently asked questions > Reserved instances > Will existing reserved instances (RIs) continue to work after the quota growth restrictions, including during redeployment, disaster recovery, or failover? :: Review disaster recovery and restore plans, modernize to newer VM generations where appropriate, and update RIs, Savings Plans, and capacity strategies to align with the target environment.

Frequently asked questions > Reserved instances > Will existing reserved instances (RIs) continue to work after the quota growth restrictions, including during redeployment, disaster recovery, or failover? :: Yes. Existing RIs remain valid through their purchased term and continue providing discounts for matching usage after quota growth restrictions take effect. Capacity growth restrictions don't invalidate existing RIs.

Frequently asked questions > What do "capacity growth restrictions" mean? :: Capacity growth restrictions mean that Azure might not approve additional quota requests, new deployments, or capacity expansion requests for impacted VM series due to limited availability of the underlying hardware. These capacity controls don't affect existing running VMs.

Frequently asked questions > What happens to quota increase requests already submitted? :: Requests submitted before enforcement took effect continue through the standard review process. Rollout timing might vary by region or system, so some customers might encounter the restriction before July 31. If you submitted the request, it proceeds through normal evaluation. If there's no option to request quota for an affected VM series, the restriction is active.
Frequently asked questions > When do capacity growth restrictions begin? :: Capacity growth restrictions for the impacted VM series begin in July 2026.

Frequently asked questions > Where can I find retirement and transition guidance for the D(s)v3 and E(s)v3 VM series? :: For the smoothest transition, see Modernize to the v5 VM series. For the latest features and performance, see Modernize to the v6 and v7 VM series.

Frequently asked questions > Where can I find retirement and transition guidance for the D(s)v3 and E(s)v3 VM series? :: The Dv3, Dsv3, Ev3, and Esv3 series retire on November 15, 2029. After that date, you can't create, resize into, run, or purchase these sizes. For retirement dates and recommended replacements, see the Retired VM sizes modernization guide.

Frequently asked questions > Why are these VM series affected? :: Azure prioritizes investment in newer-generation infrastructure that delivers improved performance, security, reliability, and platform capabilities. Older VM generations depend on hardware platforms that are no longer a focus for infrastructure expansion.

lifecycle.name: Lifecycle overview
facts: (top) :: Azure virtual machine sizes are the amount of resources allocated to a virtual machine in the cloud. These resources are a portion of the physical server’s hardware capabilities. A size series is a collection of all sizes that are available within a single physical server’s hardware. As a size series' physical hardware ages and newer components are released, Microsoft stops deploying more of previously established series' hardware. Once users modernize their workloads off that hardware or the hardware becomes sufficiently outdated, it's retired to make room for new infrastructure.

(top) :: Every Azure VM size series moves through four lifecycle stages: Current, Extended, End of Life, and Retired. Each stage tells you what to expect from a size series and what action to take. Use the lifecycle stage of your VM sizes to plan new deployments, optimize existing workloads, and schedule modernization before retirement.

Capacity restrictions :: Capacity restrictions are separate from lifecycle stages. Some older size series have capacity growth restrictions, which means Azure doesn't guarantee capacity for new or scaled-out deployments in those series. A capacity restriction isn't a retirement announcement. A series can have capacity restrictions and a separate retirement date. For example, the Dv3, Dsv3, Ev3, and Esv3 series have capacity growth restrictions that began in July 2026, and they retire on November 15, 2029.
Capacity restrictions :: For affected series and recommended alternatives, see End of Life VM size series capacity growth restrictions.

Lifecycle stages :: Current and Extended sizes are both considered modern sizes because they're fully supported. Current sizes are the newest offering in each family. When you modernize, you can move to either stage.
Lifecycle stages :: Stage | Recommended action | What to expect = Current | Adopt and expand | Recommended for new deployments and ongoing innovation.
Lifecycle stages :: Stage | Recommended action | What to expect = End of Life | Plan modernization | Retirement is announced. Prepare and complete modernization plans before the retirement date.
Lifecycle stages :: Stage | Recommended action | What to expect = Extended | Continue and evaluate | Run existing workloads while you evaluate newer options.
Lifecycle stages :: Stage | Recommended action | What to expect = Retired | Modernization completed | No longer available to create, resize into, or run.

Lifecycle stages :: The VM generations in each stage vary by VM family. For example, for general purpose sizes, v6 and v7 series are Current, v4 and v5 series are Extended, and v1 through v3 series with an announced retirement are End of Life. For other families, check the family page for the lifecycle stage of each series.

Lifecycle stages > Current :: Size series in the Current stage are the newest series in their VM family. Deploy new workloads, expand existing deployments, and optimize your Azure investments by using Current sizes.
Lifecycle stages > Current :: To modernize general purpose workloads to Current sizes, see Modernize to the v6 and v7 VM series.
Lifecycle stages > End of Life :: For a list of End of Life size series and their modernization guides, see End of Life Azure VM size series.

Lifecycle stages > End of Life :: For example, the Dv3, Dsv3, Ev3, and Esv3 series are in the End of Life stage and retire on November 15, 2029. After that date, you can't create, resize into, run, or purchase these sizes.

Lifecycle stages > End of Life :: Size series in the End of Life stage have an announced retirement. These series remain available until their retirement date, but VMs in these series have restrictions when you deploy through new subscriptions. Plan and complete your modernization to Current or Extended sizes before the retirement date.

Lifecycle stages > Extended :: If you need to modernize End of Life workloads with the least disruption, Extended sizes are a practical first step. For D-family and E-family workloads, see Modernize to the v5 VM series.

Lifecycle stages > Extended :: Size series in the Extended stage are fully supported. Continue running existing workloads on Extended sizes while you evaluate Current sizes for new deployments and future growth.

Lifecycle stages > Retired :: For a list of retired size series and their retirement dates, see Retired and retiring VM size series. For this year's retirement announcements, see Azure Virtual Machine size retirements in 2026.

Lifecycle stages > Retired :: You can't use size series in the Retired stage. At the retirement date, any remaining VMs in a retired series are deallocated, stop working, stop incurring charges, and no longer have an SLA or support.

Modernize to newer sizes :: For sizes without specific instructions, you can resize your VM to a newer size by using the Azure portal, Azure PowerShell, Azure CLI, or Terraform. Make sure that the new size supports all features that your workload requires.

Modernize to newer sizes :: For the smoothest modernization of existing workloads, see Modernize to the v5 VM series. To access the latest features and performance, see Modernize to the v6 and v7 VM series.
Modernize to newer sizes :: Modernize workloads to Current or Extended sizes. Use Current sizes for new deployments.

(top) :: The Dv3, Dsv3, Ev3, and Esv3 series retire on November 15, 2029. If you run these series, complete this transition before that date. For the smoothest transition of existing workloads, consider the v5 series first. For more information, see Modernize to the v5 VM series and What if I run Dv3, Dsv3, Ev3, or Esv3 VMs?

(top) :: The changes in this modernization affect the physical host, the virtual hardware, and the image used to create the VM. Your application, its configuration, autoscale rules, and health logic stays the same. Stateful and clustered workloads are the exception: the application itself doesn't change, but the modernization adds application-aware steps for replication and role transfer. See Discover modernization pattern by workload type.

(top) :: The v6 and v7 Azure VM series give your workloads newer, faster infrastructure with strong price-performance. Confirm platform prerequisites (boot mode, image, storage interface, network driver, and regional availability), deploy from an updated image, and validate in controlled waves.

(top) :: This article introduces the modernization and links to the detailed phases: Discover, Assess, Plan, Modernize, and Validate & optimize. It applies whether you're moving existing VMs from the v2 through v5 series or deploying greenfield.
(top) :: This modernization playbook is for architects and infrastructure teams planning a move to the v6 or v7 series, for a single workload or across a large estate.

(top) :: Consider the following factors as you plan the modernization.

(top) :: The v6 and v7 Azure VM series are built on Azure Boost and introduce a few platform changes compared with earlier generations: a Generation 2 (UEFI) foundation with Trusted Launch, NVMe-based storage, and the Microsoft Azure Network Adapter (MANA) for accelerated networking. Most workloads need only a one-time image refresh. Plan your modernization by screening each workload against the considerations in this article before you modernize.
(top) :: Workload patterns: ✔️ B. Image-based hosts · E. Customer-managed VMs · F. Stateful and clustered · G. Certified appliances — ❌ Not for A, C, or D
Commercial continuity :: How to prepare:
Commercial continuity :: Reapply Azure Hybrid Benefit and any bring-your-own-license configuration on the redeployed VM. Confirm it's set rather than assuming it transfers from the source.
Commercial continuity :: Replan or exchange reservations so discount coverage follows the workload to the new family.
Commercial continuity :: Reserved Instances and Savings Plans are scoped to a VM family, and the efficiency of the v7 series often means the same workload needs fewer or smaller vCPUs.
Commercial continuity :: Rightsize against observed usage rather than matching the old vCPU count one-for-one. This is where much of the price-performance benefit comes from.

Decide a modernization approach > Option 1. Deploy in parallel and modernize (highly recommended) :: The Microsoft recommended modernization approach is to deploy new v6 and v7 instances in parallel, then reinstall or migrate the application and data. A typical modernization wave is:

Decide a modernization approach > Option 1. Deploy in parallel and modernize (highly recommended) :: Use a controlled, wave-based approach. Confirm prerequisites, deploy from an updated image, validate the modernization, and then repeat at scale. Start with a small pilot to validate the pattern before expanding to additional workloads.
Decide a modernization approach > Option 2. In-place upgrade :: Confirm prerequisites → Back up → Convert Gen 1 to Gen 2 → Switch SCSI to NVMe → Validate → Resume workload

Decide a modernization approach > Option 2. In-place upgrade :: In some cases, you might need an in-place upgrade. This process aims to convert the VM from Generation 1 to Generation 2 and change the storage controller from SCSI to NVMe. Compared with redeployment, an in-place upgrade is more complex, has several prerequisites and steps, isn't fully compatible with all OSs and Server or VM configurations (these conditions are discussed in the following considerations in this article), requires extra careful validation, takes longer to complete, and introduces greater modernization risk. A typical modernization wave would be:

In-place upgrade :: The in-place conversion that switches an existing VM's controller from SCSI to NVMe has its own article, including setup, parameters, and how to revert. This approach has very specific requirements. Use it with caution and ensure you back up VMs. Ensure you read all the other considerations in this article. For more information, see Convert a VM from SCSI to NVMe in place.

Decide a modernization approach > Option 2. In-place upgrade :: You can't convert Generation 1 Dv2 and Dv3 VMs to Generation 2. For the full list of unsupported families, see Trusted Launch supported VM size families.

Generation 2 and Trusted Launch :: Azure Virtual Machines supports upgrading Generation 1 virtual machines (VM) to Generation 2 by upgrading to the Trusted launch security type. Enabling Trusted Launch is required.

Generation 2 and Trusted Launch :: Confirm the VM generation early. If the source is Generation 1, plan a Generation 2 image or use the in-place Generation 1 to Generation 2 upgrade, for in-place conversion.
Generation 2 and Trusted Launch :: How to prepare:
Generation 2 and Trusted Launch :: Prepare the guest OS volume.
Generation 2 and Trusted Launch :: Read carefully the compatibility and prerequisites when Disk Encryption is configured.
Generation 2 and Trusted Launch :: Review the Trusted Launch best practices.
Generation 2 and Trusted Launch :: Review the upgrade options and process for the Azure portal, PowerShell, the Azure CLI, and templates.

Generation 2 and Trusted Launch :: The v6 and v7 series use a Generation 2 (UEFI) foundation and support Trusted Launch (Secure Boot and vTPM), which is the default security type for Generation 2 VMs. Most customers modernize from the v2 or v3 series, which are often Generation 1. Sources on the v4 or v5 series are frequently Generation 2 already, so confirm the generation of each source VM early.
Generation 2 and Trusted Launch :: Trusted Launch integrates with Microsoft Defender for Cloud guest attestation, which strengthens your security baseline.

Generation 2 and Trusted Launch :: With Secure Boot enabled, make sure OS drivers and any low-level agents (antivirus, backup, or monitoring components that use kernel or filter drivers) are current and signed.
ISV virtual appliances :: Applies to: ✔️ G. Certified appliances — vendor certification is a gate, not a validation item. Confirm it before you plan anything else.

ISV virtual appliances :: Some workloads aren't just an application inside a VM, the VM is the appliance. Network virtual appliances (NVAs), Storage Appliances and others, certify specific VM families, NIC and driver configurations, and disk presentation. The move to MANA networking and an NVMe disk controller is exactly the kind of change they're sensitive to. Confirm support with the vendor before you modernize either one.

ISV virtual appliances > Confirm before you commit :: Confirm with the vendor | Why it gates the decision = Generation 2, Trusted Launch, NVMe, and MANA support | The appliance image and its drivers must handle all four.

ISV virtual appliances > Confirm before you commit :: Confirm with the vendor | Why it gates the decision = High-availability topology on the target family | The pair must be supported as a pair, not just as single instances.

ISV virtual appliances > Confirm before you commit :: Confirm with the vendor | Why it gates the decision = Licensing and bootstrap on the new size | Licenses are sometimes bound to instance attributes.

ISV virtual appliances > Confirm before you commit :: Confirm with the vendor | Why it gates the decision = Required NIC count and accelerated networking | NVAs often need a NIC layout that not every size offers.

ISV virtual appliances > Confirm before you commit :: Confirm with the vendor | Why it gates the decision = Support for the exact VM family and size | Certification is granted per family, not per generation.

The appliances that need real scrutiny are the VM-based products you run in your own subscription.

ISV virtual appliances > Storage and backup virtual appliances :: The following table lists common examples and what to confirm with each vendor. It's illustrative, not a support statement. Validate the exact product version, image, OS and driver, and target v6 or v7 size with the vendor.

ISV virtual appliances > Storage and backup virtual appliances :: Third-party storage and data-protection products often run as virtual appliances on Azure VMs (file, block, object, or backup). Because they sit directly on the VM's network and disk path, the MANA adapter and the SCSI-to-NVMe controller change can affect their drivers, throughput, and supportability, the same way they affect an NVA.

ISV virtual appliances > Storage and backup virtual appliances :: Treat VM-based storage appliances like NVAs: confirm the vendor supports the target size with the MANA adapter, an NVMe disk controller, and a Generation 2 image.
ISV virtual appliances > Storage and backup virtual appliances :: Where a managed or native Azure storage service fits, prefer it. The platform handles MANA and Boost for you.

Then reprovision and verify the extensions and agents that don't carry forward on a fresh OS disk: boot diagnostics, the monitoring or Log Analytics agent, backup integration, and any security agents.

Image prerequisites for Generation 2, NVMe, and MANA :: Inventory custom images, and confirm Generation 2, NVMe, and MANA readiness.
Image prerequisites for Generation 2, NVMe, and MANA :: Standardize on Azure Image Builder and Azure Compute Gallery with versioning, so you make the fix once and reuse it everywhere.
Image prerequisites for Generation 2, NVMe, and MANA :: Test boot and disk discovery on one VM before a broad rollout.

Image prerequisites for Generation 2, NVMe, and MANA :: The image is where Generation 2, NVMe, and MANA readiness actually live. A current marketplace image already includes all three. Custom images might need a one-time rebuild.
Local (temporary) disk behavior :: A local (temporary) disk is present only on d-suffixed sizes (for example, Ddsv6 or Ddsv7) and is presented as NVMe. Sizes without the d have no local disk.
Local (temporary) disk behavior :: How to prepare:
Local (temporary) disk behavior :: If the workload uses local scratch storage (OS page file, SQL Server tempdb, or cache), choose a d-size or relocate that data to a managed data disk.

Local (temporary) disk behavior :: On Linux, the local NVMe disk isn't auto-formatted the way the old temporary disk was, and it's re-created raw on every stop/deallocate cycle. Plan a one-time format and mount at each start if you use it, and keep nothing persistent there.
Local (temporary) disk behavior :: Treat local-disk use as a sizing decision, not an afterthought.
MANA networking :: Capture a simple before-and-after network baseline during the pilot.
MANA networking :: Confirm OS and driver readiness.
MANA networking :: How to prepare:

MANA networking :: Linux: MANA Ethernet drivers are upstream in Linux kernel 5.15 and later. Kernel 6.2 and later adds support for advanced features such as RDMA/InfiniBand and DPDK. Use a recent kernel from an endorsed distribution. For more information, see Linux VMs with the Microsoft Azure Network Adapter.
MANA networking :: Plan driver installation and validation.

MANA networking :: The v6 and v7 series use the MANA adapter, which is part of Azure Boost. This adapter includes accelerated networking. The only requirement is a current OS and driver. MANA is also rolling out to existing sizes, so this check pays off across the estate.
MANA networking :: Version floors:
MANA networking :: Windows: Current Windows Server images include the built-in driver. Keep updates applied. For more information, see Windows VMs with the Microsoft Azure Network Adapter.

NVMe storage interface :: Cross-generation upgrade often requires redeploy, not a simple VM SKU change or resize. Most v6 and v7 sizes are NVMe-only, and the disk controller type is fixed when a VM is created. The supported, predictable pattern is to redeploy from a Generation 2, NVMe-ready image, the same way image-based fleets already deploy.
NVMe storage interface :: Device paths change. Linux references such as /dev/disk/azure/scsi1/lunX no longer apply.

NVMe storage interface :: The disk controller type is fixed when a VM is created, so you can't resize a SCSI-based size directly to a remote-NVMe size. On Windows, you also can't resize between a size that has a temporary disk and one that doesn't. In both cases, redeploy from an image, or snapshot and rebuild, instead of resizing in place.
NVMe storage interface :: The v6 and v7 series present disks over NVMe. Earlier families commonly used SCSI. This change has two practical implications:

NVMe storage interface > Device paths by generation :: A v6 size can present up to four local NVMe namespaces. If you stripe or pin scratch storage to local disk, account for the new count and naming. For more information, see Local (temporary) disk behavior.

NVMe storage interface > Device paths by generation :: Any mount, script, or database setting that hard-codes an old device path points at the wrong device after modernization. Update these references to stable identifiers before you modernize.
NVMe storage interface > Device paths by generation :: Confirm the OS image includes NVMe support. See NVMe on Linux and the NVMe FAQ.
NVMe storage interface > Device paths by generation :: Disk | Pre-Boost (SCSI) | Azure Boost | v6 (NVMe) = First data disk | /dev/sdc | /dev/nvme0n2 | /dev/nvme0n2
NVMe storage interface > Device paths by generation :: Disk | Pre-Boost (SCSI) | Azure Boost | v6 (NVMe) = OS disk | /dev/sda | /dev/nvme0n1 | /dev/nvme0n1
NVMe storage interface > Device paths by generation :: Disk | Pre-Boost (SCSI) | Azure Boost | v6 (NVMe) = Temp disk count | 1 | 1 | Up to 4
NVMe storage interface > Device paths by generation :: Disk | Pre-Boost (SCSI) | Azure Boost | v6 (NVMe) = Temp disk | /dev/sdb | /dev/sda | /dev/nvme1n1
NVMe storage interface > Device paths by generation :: Disks keep their data, but the device names the OS sees change as a VM moves from SCSI to Azure Boost to a v6 size on NVMe.
NVMe storage interface > Device paths by generation :: Generation 2 VM is required for NVMe support.
NVMe storage interface > Device paths by generation :: How to prepare:
NVMe storage interface > Device paths by generation :: Plan cross-generation moves as redeploy-from-image rather than a portal resize.

NVMe storage interface > Device paths by generation :: Plan the replacement of hard-coded SCSI paths with stable identifiers, by-UUID references, filesystem labels, or Azure disk symlinks, in mount configurations, backup scripts, and database storage settings.
NVMe storage interface > Device paths by generation :: Understand the considerations around the Local Temp disk and Resize details
Next steps :: 4. Modernize: the wave-based runbook

Persistent application data on the OS disk :: A cross-generation move is usually a redeploy rather than an in-place resize, the new VM starts from a fresh OS disk built from the updated image. Any data or configuration that a workload writes directly to the OS disk, rather than to a managed data disk or an external store, doesn't carry over automatically. Some applications write state, license or activation files, configuration, or working data straight to the OS volume. Identify this content and migrate it to the new VMs after you provision them.

Persistent application data on the OS disk :: A redeploy starts from a fresh OS disk. Data that an application persists only to the OS disk, configuration, license files, local databases, or state, doesn't carry forward. Identify it up front and migrate it to the new VMs so nothing is lost.
Persistent application data on the OS disk :: Add an explicit data-migration step to your runbook: capture the OS-disk data before cutover, and restore it to the new VM after deployment.

Persistent application data on the OS disk :: Applies to: ✔️ E. Customer-managed VMs ✔️ F. Stateful and clustered ✔️ G. Certified appliances — pool-replaced and service-managed nodes hold no per-node state by design.

Persistent application data on the OS disk :: For ISV or custom applications, confirm with the vendor or development team where state is stored and whether a supported export/import or backup/restore path exists.
Persistent application data on the OS disk :: How to prepare:

Persistent application data on the OS disk :: Inventory what each workload persists to the OS disk (application configuration, license or activation files, local databases, certificates, and working or state data) versus what already lives on managed data disks or external services.

Persistent application data on the OS disk :: Keep a safety copy before you modernize. Snapshot or back up the source VM. For workloads that hold important data on the OS disk or rely on hard-coded device paths, also keep a bootable clone on a compatible older size that still uses the SCSI controller. Because the move changes the disk controller to NVMe and the device paths the OS sees, this clone gives you both a clean rollback and a running copy you can read the OS-disk data from while you copy it to the new VM.
Persistent application data on the OS disk :: Validate the migrated data and application state in the pilot before you scale to later waves.
Persistent application data on the OS disk :: Where practical, relocate persistent application data to managed data disks or external services, so future image refreshes don't require a data copy.

Persistent application data on the OS disk > Azure Disk Encryption and encryption at host :: After cutover, verify securityProfile.encryptionAtHost on the new VM, then update Key Vault access policies to disable the disk-encryption setting once nothing depends on it.

Persistent application data on the OS disk > Azure Disk Encryption and encryption at host :: An ADE-encrypted VM can't reach v6 or v7 by conversion. Encryption at host can't be enabled on a VM that currently has, or has ever had, ADE enabled, and disks previously encrypted with ADE can't use customer-managed keys. Decrypting doesn't clear it: the Unified Data Encryption (UDE) flag survives decryption, snapshots, and disk copies made with the Copy option. On Gen1 VMs, an encrypted Windows OS volume also blocks the Gen1 to Trusted Launch upgrade.

Persistent application data on the OS disk > Azure Disk Encryption and encryption at host :: Azure Disk Encryption (ADE) encrypts volumes inside the guest — BitLocker on Windows, dm-crypt on Linux — with keys held in Key Vault. It's not available on the v6 or v7 series for either operating system, and it's scheduled for retirement on 15 September 2028. After that date, ADE-enabled workloads keep running, but encrypted disks fail to unlock after a reboot.

Persistent application data on the OS disk > Azure Disk Encryption and encryption at host :: Choose the target encryption model: encryption at host with customer-managed keys for most workloads, or Confidential VM sizes with OS disk encryption where the control objective requires the platform not to handle plaintext.

Persistent application data on the OS disk > Azure Disk Encryption and encryption at host :: Confirm the target size supports encryption at host. There's no static list — retrieve the supported sizes programmatically.

Persistent application data on the OS disk > Azure Disk Encryption and encryption at host :: Domain-joined VMs: remove the VM from the domain before deleting the original, and rejoin afterward. The replacement has a different computer SID, which affects anything bound to machine identity.
Persistent application data on the OS disk > Azure Disk Encryption and encryption at host :: Downtime. The disk copy and VM recreation can't be done online.

Persistent application data on the OS disk > Azure Disk Encryption and encryption at host :: Fold the rebuild into the modernization wave rather than running it as a separate project. It's the same work, and it's required before the 2028 retirement regardless.
Persistent application data on the OS disk > Azure Disk Encryption and encryption at host :: For the full procedure, see Migrate from Azure Disk Encryption to encryption at host.
Persistent application data on the OS disk > Azure Disk Encryption and encryption at host :: How to prepare:
Persistent application data on the OS disk > Azure Disk Encryption and encryption at host :: Inventory which VMs have ADE enabled, and whether the OS disk, the data disks, or both are encrypted.

Persistent application data on the OS disk > Azure Disk Encryption and encryption at host :: Linux with an encrypted OS disk: ADE can't be disabled. Build a new VM from a current image and migrate data at the application level. There's no disk-copy path.

Persistent application data on the OS disk > Azure Disk Encryption and encryption at host :: New disks and a new VM. There's no in-place conversion. Create the target disk by using the upload method and copy the VHD blob. Add a 512-byte offset because Azure omits the footer when it reports disk size.

Persistent application data on the OS disk > Azure Disk Encryption and encryption at host :: The replacement is encryption at host, which encrypts on the host before data reaches storage. Resume hibernated VMs before you modernize :: A VM in the hibernated state holds a saved memory image. While it stays there, you can't resize it, attach or detach disks, or change NICs.
Resume hibernated VMs before you modernize :: A VM with hibernation only enabled, sitting in Running or Stop (deallocated), resizes normally.

Resume hibernated VMs before you modernize :: A move to v6 or v7 is a redeploy or a VM Generation and disk-controller conversion. Neither path carries a saved memory state forward, so you must resume and clear the hibernated image first.

Resume hibernated VMs before you modernize :: Applies to: ✔️ E. Customer-managed VMs, including Azure Virtual Desktop personal host pools — pooled session hosts and service-managed compute don't hibernate.

Resume hibernated VMs before you modernize :: Azure VM hibernation performs a suspend-to-disk: Azure stores the VM's memory contents on the OS disk and then deallocates the VM. It's common for virtual desktops and dev/test servers that don't run all day. Two states behave differently:

Resume hibernated VMs before you modernize :: Check virtualization-based security (VBS). If the workload uses Device Guard or Credential Guard, hibernation also requires Trusted Launch and Nested Virtualization. On Windows 11 24H2, that combination requires OS build 26100.3037 or later. Re-validate whenever the image or VM generation changes.
Resume hibernated VMs before you modernize :: How to prepare:

Resume hibernated VMs before you modernize :: Plan the resume step as a capacity risk. Hibernated VMs carry no capacity guarantee on resume, and capacity reservations don't cover them. Bringing a VDI pool back at once depends on available capacity in the target region and zone. See Region, zone, and capacity planning.

Resume hibernated VMs before you modernize :: Re-enable hibernation on the new VM. Deallocate it, set supportsHibernation=true on the OS disk, run az vm update --enable-hibernation true, then reconfigure the guest OS. The OS disk must be large enough to hold the memory contents plus the OS, so a larger-memory size might need a larger OS disk. On Windows, the page file must be on the OS disk (C:), not the temporary disk.

Resume hibernated VMs before you modernize :: Re-validate hibernation support on the exact v6 or v7 target. Support is gated by both VM size and a RAM ceiling, up to 64 GB on supported general-purpose series and up to 112 GB on supported GPU series. As of this writing, the documented hibernation-supported sizes are v5-series general-purpose families (Dasv5, Dadsv5, Dsv5, Ddsv5, Easv5, Eadsv5, Esv5, Edsv5) and the NVv4 and NVadsA10v5 GPU series, no v6 or v7 sizes are listed yet. Confirm the specific target on the supported-sizes list before you rely on hibernation.

Resume hibernated VMs before you modernize :: Resume a hibernated VM and reach Stop (deallocated) before you modernize. The saved session state stays on the old VM and is discarded, so save anything important first. Re-enable hibernation on the new size only after you confirm the size supports it and the OS disk can hold the new memory image.

Resume hibernated VMs before you modernize :: Resume, then modernize. The working path is: resume (unhibernate) so the saved memory state is restored, let the workload settle, shut down to Stop (deallocated), then convert or redeploy and restart. A guest-OS shutdown alone isn't enough, the resize, disk, and NIC blocks clear only after the VM leaves the hibernated state and reaches Stop (deallocated).

Resume hibernated VMs before you modernize :: Treat the memory image as throwaway. It doesn't transfer to the new VM, so confirm anything important is written to a disk or an external store before you resume and cut over.

What changes when the VM family changes :: Availability and commercial planning: Confirm regional and zonal availability, quota, and capacity. Review reservations, savings plans, licensing, and any family-specific commercial commitments before the transition.

What changes when the VM family changes :: Boot generation: The D-family and E-family v5 series support both Generation 1 and Generation 2 VMs. A generation change isn't normally required for a resize. When you rebuild or refresh the image, consider Generation 2 and Trusted Launch.
What changes when the VM family changes :: Focus planning on the platform characteristics that can affect workload behavior:
What changes when the VM family changes :: Image and operating system: Confirm that the operating system is supported and current. Refresh older images and guest drivers before a broad transition.

What changes when the VM family changes :: Local temporary storage: Many base v5 series, including Dv5, Dsv5, Dasv5, Ev5, Esv5, and Easv5, don't include a local temporary disk. Select a d variant when the workload requires local scratch space. Never place persistent data on the temporary disk.

What changes when the VM family changes :: Networking: Accelerated Networking is required on the Intel D-family v5 series (Dv5, Dsv5, Ddv5, and Ddsv5) and supported on the AMD and E-family v5 series. Enable Accelerated Networking on the source VM before you resize to a series that requires it. Use a supported OS image and current drivers, and compare NIC count and expected bandwidth with the source size.

What changes when the VM family changes :: Processor performance: Newer-generation processors provide improved performance. Validate performance against your workload baseline before you select the final size.

What changes when the VM family changes :: Storage performance: Storage performance increased significantly with v5. It's generally less of a concern unless the vCPU count changes substantially between the current and target sizes.

facts: (top) :: Azure Disk Encryption is scheduled for retirement on September 15, 2028. Until that date, you can continue to use Azure Disk Encryption without disruption. On September 15, 2028, ADE-enabled workloads will continue to run, but encrypted disks will fail to unlock after VM reboots, resulting in service disruption.

(top) :: This article provides step-by-step guidance for migrating your virtual machines from Azure Disk Encryption (ADE) to encryption at host. The migration process requires creating new disks and VMs because in-place conversion isn't supported.

(top) :: Use encryption at host for new VMs, or consider Confidential VM sizes with OS disk encryption for confidential computing workloads. All ADE-enabled VMs (including backups) must migrate to encryption at host before the retirement date to avoid service disruption. See Migrate from Azure Disk Encryption to encryption at host for details.

(top) :: Read more about the B-series CPU credit model.

(top) :: The 'B' family of VM size series are one of Azure's general purpose VM instances. While traditional Azure virtual machines provide fixed CPU performance, B-series virtual machines are the only VM type that use credits for CPU performance provisioning. B-series VMs utilize a CPU credit model to track how much CPU is consumed - the virtual machine accumulates CPU credits when a workload is operating below the base CPU performance threshold and uses credits when running above the base CPU performance threshold until all of its credits are consumed. Upon consuming all the CPU credits, a B-series virtual machine is throttled back to its base CPU performance until it accumulates the credits to CPU burst again.

Series in family > Basv2-series :: Basv2-series virtual machines offer a balance of compute, memory, and network resources, and are a cost effective way to run a broad spectrum of general purpose workloads. These include large scale micro-services, small and medium databases, virtual desktops, and business-critical applications. This series also offers an affordable option to run your code repositories and dev/test environments. Basv2-Series offers virtual machines of up-to 32 vCPU and 128 Gib of RAM, with max network bandwidth of upto 6,250 Mbps and max uncached disk throughput of 600 Mbps. Basv2-series virtual machines also support attachments of Standard SSD, Standard HDD, Premium SSD types with a default Remote-SSD support. You can also attach Ultra Disk storage based on its regional availability. Disk storage is billed separately from virtual machines.

Series in family > Basv2-series :: Basv2-series virtual machines run on the AMD's third Generation EPYC™ 7763v processor in a multi-threaded configuration with up to 256 MB L3 cache configuration. This series provides low cost CPU burstable general purpose virtual machines. Basv2-series virtual machines utilize a CPU credit model to track how much CPU is consumed. The virtual machine accumulates CPU credits when a workload is operating below the base CPU performance threshold and uses credits when running above the base CPU performance threshold, until all of its credits are consumed. Upon consuming all the CPU credits, a Basv2-series virtual machine is throttled back to its base CPU performance until it accumulates the credits to CPU burst again.

Series in family > Bpsv2-series :: The Bpsv2-series virtual machines are based on the Arm architecture, featuring the Ampere® Altra® Arm-based processor operating at 3.0 GHz, delivering outstanding price-performance for general-purpose workloads. These virtual machines offer a range of VM sizes, from 0.5 GiB to up to 4 GiB of memory per vCPU, to meet the needs of applications that don't need the full performance of the CPU continuously, such as development and test servers, low traffic web servers, small databases, micro services, servers for proof-of-concepts, build servers, and code repositories. These workloads typically have burstable performance requirements. The Bpsv2-series VMs provides you with the ability to purchase a VM size with baseline performance that can build up credits when it's using less than its baseline performance. When the VM has accumulated credits, the VM can burst above the baseline using up to 100% of the vCPU when your application requires higher CPU performance.

ddv4.name: Ddv4 series
facts: (top) :: The Ddv4 and Ddsv4-series run on the Intel® Xeon® Platinum 8573C (Emerald Rapids), Intel® Xeon® Platinum 8370C (Ice Lake) or the Intel® Xeon® Platinum 8272CL (Cascade Lake) processors in a hyper-threaded configuration, providing a better value proposition for most general-purpose workloads. It features an all core Turbo clock speed of 3.4 GHz, Intel® Turbo Boost Technology 2.0, Intel® Hyper-Threading Technology and Intel® Advanced Vector Extensions 512 (Intel® AVX-512). They also support Intel® Deep Learning Boost. These new VM sizes will have 50% larger local storage, as well as better local disk IOPS for both read and write compared to the Dv3/Dsv3 sizes with Gen2 VMs. D-series use cases include enterprise-grade applications, relational databases, in-memory caching, and analytics.

ev5.name: Ev5 series
facts: (top) :: Ev5-series supports Standard SSD, Standard HDD, and Premium SSD types. You can also attach Ultra Disk storage based on its regional availability. Disk storage is billed separately from virtual machines.

(top) :: Ev5-series virtual machines run on Intel® Xeon® Platinum 8573C (Emerald Rapids), Intel® Xeon® Platinum 8473C (Sapphire Rapids) or Intel® Xeon® Platinum 8370C (Ice Lake) processor in a hyper threaded configuration. This new processor features an all core turbo clock speed of 3.5 GHz with Intel® Turbo Boost Technology, Intel® Advanced-Vector Extensions 512 (Intel® AVX-512) and Intel® Deep Learning Boost. These virtual machines offer up to 104 vCPU and 672 GiB of RAM. Esv5-series virtual machines don't have temporary storage thus lowering the price of entry.

capacity-resilience.name: Well-Architected Framework: capacity resilience
facts: (top) :: All cloud hyperscalers operate within the physical infrastructure available to support their services, including datacenter space, servers, networking, power, and cooling. As demand nears available supply, constraints can affect resource allocation and deployment, making proactive capacity planning a non-negotiable exercise.
(top) :: Cloud computing is often described as elastic because of its ability to scale workloads and consume infrastructure without worrying about underlying hardware.

(top) :: This article covers architectural approaches and Azure capabilities that can proactively help you plan for capacity and minimize those issues during deployment. This article doesn't provide troubleshooting guidance or short term-mitigations. For that information, see Troubleshoot allocation failures when you create or resize VMs in Azure.

Adopt a shared responsibility model :: As part of your responsibility, design your workload to judiciously use what's available. You're responsible for forecasting your capacity, designing flexible architectures, and reserving or requesting capacity before you need it. For capacity planning strategies, see Make capacity planning an ongoing operational practice.

Adopt a shared responsibility model :: Availability is also point-in-time and request-specific. Releasing resources or changing deployment constraints can change the outcome of a subsequent allocation request, even when the request uses the same region, zone, and service or VM family.

Adopt a shared responsibility model :: Cloud hyperscalers continually expand infrastructure and provide capabilities that improve resource allocation and deployment success. However, capacity management is best treated as a shared responsibility between the cloud provider and its customers.

Adopt a shared responsibility model :: Microsoft is responsible for expanding and maintaining regional infrastructure to support customer demands. It also uses capacity-management controls to reduce noisy-neighbor effects. For example, Azure can detect demand spikes and apply resource controls that help prevent a single resource's sudden increase in usage from affecting shared capacity.

Common antipatterns and alternatives :: Antipattern | Risk | Recommended alternative = Delaying capacity reservations until critical | Provisioning reservations only when workloads become business-critical misses opportunities for proactive planning and increases deployment risk during growth events. | Pre-provision capacity for critical workloads, use phased provisioning for large requests, and reserve headroom before growth events.

Common antipatterns and alternatives :: Antipattern | Risk | Recommended alternative = Hoarding reserved capacity within teams | Teams hold unused capacity while others are limited in their deployments. This fragmentation prevents optimal allocation. | Manage reservations centrally and share capacity reservation groups across subscriptions to improve utilization and response flexibility.

Common antipatterns and alternatives :: Antipattern | Risk | Recommended alternative = Not anticipating allocation failures | Scale-out or replacement operations can fail unexpectedly, causing performance degradation or availability impact when workloads rely on new instances. | Design for the possibility that new instances can't be allocated when needed because of capacity pressures. Use throttling, queues, retries, and degraded operation to continue serving requests when scale-out is delayed or fails. Verify that new instances are healthy and ready before directing traffic or depending on their capacity.

Common antipatterns and alternatives :: Antipattern | Risk | Recommended alternative = Reactive scaling without capacity planning | Autoscaling might trigger successfully but fail to provision additional resources, resulting in degraded application performance or availability during peak demand. | Run ongoing capacity planning with forecasts, quota checks, and early requests; set quota alerts and finalize major capacity needs at least eight weeks before activation.

Common antipatterns and alternatives :: Antipattern | Risk | Recommended alternative = Single-region deployment as the primary model | Relies on a single regional capacity pool. Regional outages or capacity issues prevent deployments, scaling, and disaster recovery. | Adopt multi-region architecture as the default resilience boundary, targeting three regions as a baseline and four or more for large enterprises.

Common antipatterns and alternatives :: Antipattern | Risk | Recommended alternative = Treating quota as immutable team boundaries | Separate quotas per team or subscription create silos; dynamic pooling allows capacity to flow where needed most. | Treat quota as a dynamic pool by using Azure Quota Groups and reassigning quota based on changing workload demand.

Common antipatterns and alternatives :: Antipattern | Risk | Recommended alternative = Using only one SKU or instance type | High-demand or specialized SKUs can become constrained, preventing deployment or scale-out even when alternatives exist. | Design fungible deployments across compatible SKUs and use services like Compute Fleet, flexible VMSS, or AKS auto-provisioning to avoid SKU lock-in.

Common antipatterns and alternatives :: Antipattern | Risk | Recommended alternative = Zone-pinned deployment | Creates a dependency on a single availability zone, eliminating alternatives during outages or capacity shortages. | Remove unnecessary zone pinning, use zone-resilient deployments where possible, and keep alternate zone options ready for constrained events.
Common antipatterns and alternatives :: This section highlights common antipatterns to watch for and alternatives that can help you build more resilient, flexible deployments.

Design for zone flexibility :: Consider a two-zone deployment strategy, where supported. Depending on the service, a two-zone deployment can meet availability targets without using every availability zone in a region. Confirm the applicable SLA for each service. Services such as Azure VMs and some eligible PaaS services (see Azure services that support availability zones) can run in a two-zone configuration while maintaining their documented SLA and availability guarantees. When a single availability zone experiences capacity degradation, a two-zone deployment can help maintain availability targets while improving deployment flexibility.

Make capacity planning an ongoing operational practice :: Capacity planning must be a continuous operational discipline. Estimate the CPU, memory, storage, and network bandwidth needed to support current and anticipated demand. Apart from independent raw metrics from resources, also express capacity requirements for scale units and deployment stamps that include all resources in the unit.
Make capacity planning an ongoing operational practice :: For key strategies, see PE:02: Architecture strategies for capacity planning.

Make capacity planning an ongoing operational practice :: Plan with sufficient lead time for the slowest dependencies. Factor in time for obtaining region access, enabling availability zones, and setting up capacity reservations.

Make capacity planning an ongoing operational practice :: Start capacity planning with questions like "How do we recover?" to "What capacity will we need next month, next quarter, or during our next growth event, and what will it cost if we forecast it early rather than wait until we need it?"

Make capacity planning an ongoing operational practice :: This factor is also a cost decision. Use those demand forecasts to guide reservations and savings plans, so you can lock in capacity and pricing before a constrained peak forces premium pay-as-you-go rates. Be aware that cost can vary by region.

Make capacity planning an ongoing operational practice > Optimize, govern, and automate :: Configure quota alerts at meaningful utilization thresholds, such as 70%, 85%, and 95%, to identify potential issues before they affect deployments.
Make capacity planning an ongoing operational practice > Optimize, govern, and automate :: Ensure your subscriptions have quota and access policies configured in advance of production deployment.

Make capacity planning an ongoing operational practice > Optimize, govern, and automate :: Start capacity planning at the individual workload level, then expand it across business units and workload portfolios as your cloud adoption grows.

Make capacity planning an ongoing operational practice > Optimize, govern, and automate :: Treat allocation failures as operational signals that indicate emerging capacity pressure, rather than isolated deployment anomalies. Observe trends in allocation failures to act early when a workload or region is approaching its capacity limits.

Make capacity planning an ongoing operational practice > Place workloads and secure capacity :: Preserve subscriptions that already have access to restricted regions or specialized SKUs instead of deleting and recreating them. Consider using Azure Quota Groups that allow you to self-manage and share quota among a group of subscriptions. For example, use quota groups to reclaim unused quota from a subscription and keep the cores in a private quota pool for use by another subscription.

Make capacity planning an ongoing operational practice > Place workloads and secure capacity :: Risk: Requesting new access to constrained regions adds more competition for the same finite capacity. Preserve existing access and share it instead of requesting new access.

Make capacity planning an ongoing operational practice > Place workloads and secure capacity :: Start capacity planning early and refine forecasts throughout the planning phase. Finalize capacity before activation and allow time for quota requests, region access approvals, and capacity reservations. Apply reservations and savings plans as soon as practical after resources are created, track commitment coverage to avoid overpurchasing, and coordinate with operations teams to avoid surprises when workloads are offboarded.

Make capacity planning an ongoing operational practice > Plan and forecast demand :: Build demand forecasts by using production telemetry, historical growth trends, and planned onboarding activities. Include temporary demand from upgrades, replacements, and failover. For example, AKS and VMSS surge operations create extra instances and consume quota and capacity while the operation is in progress.
Make capacity planning an ongoing operational practice > Plan and forecast demand :: Track capacity requirements by service or SKU family, region, availability zone, and dependent services.

Pre-provision capacity intentionally :: A common reactive pattern is to provision infrastructure first and request quota only when needed. This approach assumes Azure can allocate capacity within minutes or hours, which might not hold when capacity is constrained. Forecast demand from expected growth, planned deployments, seasonal events, and other drivers, then:

Pre-provision capacity intentionally :: Classify workloads and flows by criticality. Workload components that are business-critical should be supported with pre-provisioned capacity. Other flows can use flexible architecture, reducing unnecessary capacity costs. For more information, see Identify critical flows.
Pre-provision capacity intentionally :: Do eligibility checks and identify unsupported GPU/HPC families, Spot VMs, availability sets, dedicated hosts, and other constraints.
Pre-provision capacity intentionally :: For business-critical workloads, paying for reserved headroom is often less expensive than the operational and financial impact of capacity shortages.

Pre-provision capacity intentionally :: For regional (nonzonal) VMs, you can still associate them with capacity reservations, but the VM must be deallocated and reallocated to the capacity reservation group. For more information, see Associate an existing virtual machine.

Pre-provision capacity intentionally :: For workloads with predictable or business-critical capacity requirements, consider Azure Capacity Reservations. This capability reserves VM compute capacity in a specific Azure region or availability zone. To create the reservation, you must have subscription quota and capacity available. If there's already an outage or capacity shortage, don't assume you can create a reservation at that moment to solve the problem. Plan in advance.
Pre-provision capacity intentionally :: Reserve capacity for compute resources that are critical for your workload.

Pre-provision capacity intentionally :: Reserve capacity where the cost of not having it is greater than the cost of keeping it idle. Evaluate factors such as the cost per tenant, cost per application stamp, and the business impact of specific scenarios. For example, consider the impact of delaying a large migration, missing a customer onboarding deadline, or being unable to scale a SaaS service.

Pre-provision capacity intentionally :: Reserved Instances and Savings Plans optimize cost. Capacity Reservations secure capacity availability. These mechanisms can be combined, allowing organizations to reserve capacity while still benefiting from existing commitment discounts.

Pre-provision capacity intentionally :: Tradeoff: Capacity reservations involve a cost tradeoff. You pay for reserved capacity even when it isn't being used because Azure is holding those resources for your workload.

Pre-provision capacity intentionally :: Use a phased provisioning approach for large capacity requests. Instead of requesting all capacity at once, provision incrementally in stages (for example, 25% stages for a 2,000 vCPU request).

Pre-provision capacity intentionally :: Validate region and availability zone access, subscription quota, SKU availability, service dependencies, and recent deployment test results in your target locations. Identify fallback zones, regions, and alternative SKUs in advance. Because capacity is allocated only at deployment time, capacity reservations are suitable for workloads that require guaranteed VM capacity.

Pre-provision capacity intentionally :: You can associate an existing zonal VM with a capacity reservation without redeploying or reallocating the VM. For example, if you deployed 100 zonal VMs in East US, Zone 1, and the workload later becomes business critical, you can attach them to capacity reservations to protect against capacity shortages during future changes.
Prefer fungible VM deployments :: Azure makes placement decisions, so you can focus on your functional and nonfunctional requirements.

Prefer fungible VM deployments :: Containerized workloads: Use Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) auto-provisioning to automatically provision nodes across multiple VM types and zones based on workload requirements, eliminating manual SKU pinning.

Prefer fungible VM deployments :: Design workloads to support multiple compatible VM SKUs instead of pinning to a single series. Consider using Azure Compute Fleet, a capacity orchestration service that abstracts SKU selection. You specify your compute capacity needs; Compute Fleet automatically selects the optimal combination of VM types, availability zones, and pricing. Keep in mind that quotas still apply per subscription, region, and VM family.

Prefer fungible VM deployments :: Higher deployment success rates by using available capacity pools.
Prefer fungible VM deployments :: Potential cost optimization through mix and match of compatible VM families.

Prefer fungible VM deployments :: Reduced operational overhead from SKU management. Instead of managing quotas for hundreds of individual VM series, adopt vCPU-based quota categories that support capacity-first deployment.
Prefer fungible VM deployments :: This infrastructure abstraction provides key benefits:

Prefer fungible VM deployments :: Web and application server scaling: Use Virtual Machine Scale Sets (VMSS) with flexible orchestration to deploy mixed VM types within a single scale set. Azure automatically distributes instances across SKUs and zones based on availability.

Prioritize multi-region design over single-region deployments :: Adding a new region doesn't automatically require a full networking stack in that region. In many multi-region designs, you can use global connectivity, peering, and centralized shared services instead of duplicating a full hub-and-spoke deployment in every region.
Prioritize multi-region design over single-region deployments :: Availability of the Azure services, features, and zones that the workload requires.
Prioritize multi-region design over single-region deployments :: Capacity and SKU availability for current and anticipated workload requirements.
Prioritize multi-region design over single-region deployments :: Data residency, sovereignty, and compliance requirements.

Prioritize multi-region design over single-region deployments :: Deployment pattern | Availability model | Example target availability = Multi-region | Protects against zone and regional outage and capacity limitations, assuming failover automation and data replication | ~99.99% +

Prioritize multi-region design over single-region deployments :: Deployment pattern | Availability model | Example target availability = Multi-zone | Protects against zone failure with redundant placement across zones | ~99.95% to 99.99%

Prioritize multi-region design over single-region deployments :: Deployment pattern | Availability model | Example target availability = Single zone | Protects against host or rack failure, but not zone loss or regional disruption | ~99.9%

Prioritize multi-region design over single-region deployments :: Don't rely solely on a primary region and its Azure-paired region, if it has one. If the paired region experiences the same failure as the primary region, it might not have sufficient capacity to absorb failover demand. This condition can make it harder to meet availability and disaster recovery objectives. Paired regions work well for blob storage with GRS (Geo-Redundant Storage) because Microsoft handles replication, but they aren't suitable as the sole capacity strategy for compute workloads that you manage directly, such as VMs, AKS, and App Service.

Prioritize multi-region design over single-region deployments :: For more information about regional availability strategies, see Using Availability Zones and Regions and Develop a disaster recovery plan for multi-region deployments.
Prioritize multi-region design over single-region deployments :: Performance characteristics, including cross-region replication and network egress.
Prioritize multi-region design over single-region deployments :: Reliability and recovery targets.
Prioritize multi-region design over single-region deployments :: Select regions based on these factors:

Prioritize multi-region design over single-region deployments :: Single-region can be appropriate for workloads with modest growth requirements, low availability needs, strict data residency requirements that only a single Azure region can meet, or a strong preference for operational simplicity. Confirm that the region and services you select can support anticipated growth and recovery requirements. It provides no regional fallback, so choose it deliberately when the workload requirements and operating model support that constraint.

Prioritize multi-region design over single-region deployments :: Start with a multi-region approach. You don't need to deploy every application to every region. For example, App A can run active-active in regions 1 and 2 for high volume and low latency, App B in regions 2 and 3 for geographic diversity, and App C in regions 3 and 4 for a different user base. This distribution spreads load across regional capacity pools, which have different utilization profiles.
Prioritize multi-region design over single-region deployments :: The cost and operational complexity of deploying, monitoring, securing, and recovering the workload across regions.
Prioritize multi-region design over single-region deployments :: The right number of regions depends on your workload requirements and operating model:

Prioritize multi-region design over single-region deployments :: This table shows the common deployment patterns for a three-tier application. These numbers are illustrative and depend on workload architecture, dependencies, and recovery automation.

Prioritize multi-region design over single-region deployments :: Three or more regions provides stronger protection. This approach can be appropriate for larger or business-critical workloads. When one region is constrained, two others remain available for capacity and failover. If one region experiences capacity pressure, the other two remain available to support capacity needs and failover. For most medium-scale organizations, consider this as the baseline strategy. Evaluate the benefits against business requirements like data residency, operational complexity, cost, and others.
Prioritize multi-region design over single-region deployments :: Tolerated latency between users, application components, data stores, and dependent services.

Prioritize multi-region design over single-region deployments :: Tradeoff: A multi-region architecture improves resilience but it also introduces tradeoffs. Replicating data across regions can increase latency and data egress costs, while data residency and sovereignty requirements may restrict where data can be stored or replicated. Operating across multiple regions also increases architectural and operational complexity, requiring additional mechanisms for replication, failover, monitoring, and consistency management.

Prioritize multi-region design over single-region deployments :: Treat Azure as a global platform with multiple regional capacity pools. Each region has a carrying capacity based on available space, power, cooling, and other factors, which defines how much it can absorb. Deployment approaches such as single-region, paired-region passive (where available), or two-region active-active are still valid, but they might not be sufficient when it comes to building capacity resilience. A multi-region design gives your workload more flexibility by giving it access to extra capacity pools and deployment locations.

Prioritize multi-region design over single-region deployments :: Two regions provide an extra capacity pool and can support active-passive or active-active designs. This design can be appropriate for noncritical or lightly distributed workloads that need regional failover but can tolerate the risk that both regions experience capacity pressure at the same time.

Prioritize multi-region design over single-region deployments :: You can expand even more. Four or more regions are recommended for large enterprises. It maximizes capacity, geographic proximity to users, and resilience against regional outages or constraints.

Share reserved capacity :: Manage reservations centrally and share them across business units, subscriptions, and workloads where needed. Consider using passive DR infrastructure to support analytics workloads, generating grounding data for AI, and performing other compute-intensive work that doesn't need to be done in real time. This approach also aligns with the Cost Optimization principle of use what you pay for.

Share reserved capacity :: When teams or workloads manage reserved capacity independently, it can be underutilized while other business units have unmet deployment requirements. Disaster recovery (DR) capacity can also remain idle for long periods.

Terminology :: Term | Definition = Azure Quota Groups | An organizational feature that allows self-management and sharing of quota across multiple subscriptions, enabling dynamic reallocation based on workload demand rather than treating quota as siloed team boundaries.
