Terminology :: Term | Definition = Capacity | The amount of underlying physical infrastructure (datacenters, servers, networking, power, cooling) available in a specific region, availability zone, or cluster for a requested resource.

Terminology :: Term | Definition = On-demand Capacity Reservation (ODCR) | A feature that reserves VM compute capacity in a specific region or availability zone, guaranteeing capacity for critical workloads. Combines with Reserved Instances or Savings Plans for cost optimization.
Terminology :: Term | Definition = Quota | A policy on how many resources your subscription can request in a given region and SKU family.

Terminology :: Term | Definition = Zone resiliency | A deployment strategy where resources are spread across multiple availability zones within a region to protect against zone outages or capacity limitations.
Treat quota as a dynamic pool :: Organizations often treat Azure subscriptions as permanent organizational boundaries. Instead, treat them as containers for acquiring and managing quota.
Treat quota as a dynamic pool :: Quota Groups reallocate quota between member subscriptions; they don't guarantee physical capacity.

Treat quota as a dynamic pool :: Use Azure Quota Groups to self-manage and share quota across subscriptions. They're particularly valuable for Enterprise Agreement (EA) customers, allowing approved quota to move across business units instead of remaining siloed in subscriptions with constrained limits.
Understand quota and capacity :: Availability zone level: A single availability zone might run out of capacity for a specific SKU while other zones in the same region remain unaffected.

Understand quota and capacity :: Capacity is supply. It's the amount of underlying infrastructure available in a specific region or availability zone for the exact resource configuration being requested.

Understand quota and capacity :: Capacity-related deployment issues can occur at multiple scopes as shown in this image. Azure capacity is distributed across a large global pool, but each scope such as region, zone, service, VM family and SKU, or cluster placement rule narrows the set of valid targets for a deployment.

Understand quota and capacity :: Quota is the policy. It limits how many resources your subscription can consume in a given region and SKU family. For example, if your subscription has a quota of 100 vCPUs in East US, you can provision up to 100 vCPUs in that region.
Understand quota and capacity :: Region level: An entire region might be constrained for a particular service or VM SKU, leaving no available capacity regardless of the zone selected.

Understand quota and capacity :: SKU level: Capacity can be limited to specific hardware or service offerings. For example, high-demand GPU instances or newly introduced VM families might be constrained, while other SKUs remain readily available.
Understand quota and capacity :: Two distinct concepts control resource allocation in Azure: quota and capacity. Both must align for successful deployment.
Understand quota and capacity :: Understand which scopes need flexibility so that you improve the chances of a successful deployment.
Understand quota and capacity :: Unlike quota, capacity can only increase if the platform acquires more infrastructure.

Understand quota and capacity :: You can increase the resource limits assigned to your Azure subscription through quota requests. The system typically processes standard requests automatically and completes them quickly. For constrained resources, the system reviews requests manually. Large requests or requests in constrained regions can take longer to approve. Microsoft works with you through your support case to identify the best path forward.
What are allocation failures? :: Allocation failures occur when you have sufficient quota but physical capacity isn't available.

What are allocation failures? :: During those events, you might see deployment failures with errors like AllocationFailed or ZonalAllocationFailed. You might also see SKU unavailability messages for a particular zone. For more information about allocation failures, see Troubleshoot allocation failures when you create or resize VMs in Azure.

What are allocation failures? :: Those failures might be triggered by a particular combination of resource, configuration, and location, which can't be provisioned at a given moment. They usually appear during moments of change. For example, when you scale out during demand growth, resize or upgrade VM families, or during in-place updates.

What are allocation failures? :: When Microsoft detects capacity constraints that could affect your workloads, you are alerted through Azure Service Health with details about the issue, potential alternatives, and expected timelines for resolution. Alerts are only triggered for actual allocation failures. Service Health alerts are just one signal; they don't guarantee that a specific allocation request will succeed.

What are allocation failures? :: When you see these errors, start by asking: Is the failure limited to one zone, all zones in a region, one SKU family, a managed-service dependency, or the subscription itself? A thorough analysis should lead you to the next move: a quota request, a region or zone access request, a different deployment shape, or an architectural change. The following sections focus on the architectural strategies that can prevent these failures.

facts: (top) :: Azure continues to support the SCSI interface on the VM offerings that provide SCSI storage. However, not all new VM series include SCSI as an option going forward.

(top) :: Azure virtual machines (VMs) support two storage controller interfaces: Small Computer System Interface (SCSI) and NVM Express (NVMe). SCSI is a legacy standard that provides physical connectivity and data transfer between computers and peripheral devices. NVMe provides similar connectivity, but is a faster and more efficient interface for data transfer between servers and storage systems.
(top) :: Linux and Windows VMs.
(top) :: This article shows you how to convert an Azure VM from a SCSI disk controller to NVMe by using Azure Boost and the Azure NVMe Conversion script. The same script and procedure apply to:
(top) :: VMs with or without data disks and a temporary disk.

What's changing for your VM? > tab linux :: Disk | SCSI VM | NVMe VM (v5 with temp disk) | NVMe VM (v6) = Temp disk | /dev/sdb | /dev/sda | /dev/nvme1n1

What's changing for your VM? > tab windows :: Converting your Azure VM from SCSI to NVMe by using Azure Boost can help you take full advantage of these performance improvements and maintain a competitive edge in the cloud computing landscape.

What's changing for your VM? > tab windows :: Disk | SCSI VM | NVMe VM = OS disk | C:\ | C:\

What's changing for your VM? > tab windows :: On v6 SKUs, temp disks are RAW and aren't preformatted with NTFS. Use a startup script or custom script extension to format and mount them at each startup.
What's changing for your VM? > tab windows :: Some VM sizes (for example, Standard_E64ds_v6) have more than one temporary disk.

What's changing for your VM? > tab windows :: Windows uses drive letters rather than device paths, so the OS disk stays C:\ after conversion. The underlying disk interface changes. Data disk assignments might shift if you don't use persistent disk identifiers.

scsi-to-nvme.name: Convert a VM from SCSI to NVMe in place
facts: (top) :: Applies to: ✔️ Linux VMs ✔️ Windows VMs
(top) :: For the platform reference behind the conversion, how the disk controller type changes and how to verify the result, see Convert SCSI to NVMe for Linux and Windows VMs.

(top) :: The conversion script is a community utility published by the SAP on Azure team in the Azure/SAP-on-Azure-Scripts-and-Utilities repository. Microsoft doesn't consider the script an officially supported product, service, or tool. The SAP on Azure team provides the script as-is. Review the script carefully, and test it in a non-production environment first. Pair it with the runbook sequence and the readiness assessment so you run it with a backup and a rollback already in hand.

(top) :: The wave-based runbook covers the full modernization sequence. This page focuses on the tool that does the in-place work: a script that switches a VM's disk controller between SCSI and NVMe without a rebuild, so the existing OS disk is kept.

(top) :: This script is for no-temp-disk source VMs only, sizes without a d before the version suffix (for example, Standard_D4s_v5 or Standard_D8s_v5). VMs that already have a local temporary disk (for example, Standard_D4ds_v5) can convert in place to a v6 size as long as you enable the preview feature VMTempDiskResizePreview ; use the redeploy-from-image path instead. See the temporary-disk dependency row in the readiness assessment.

Before you run the conversion :: Azure Disk Encryption (ADE) for Linux. ADE for Linux isn't supported with NVMe, so converting an ADE-encrypted Linux VM produces an unsupported configuration. Check for ADE yourself and decrypt the VM first (or use the redeploy-from-image path). The current script doesn't detect ADE and can complete without warning, leaving the VM in an unsupported state.
Before you run the conversion :: Confirm the following on the source VM. Each one produces an unsupported result if you skip it:
Before you run the conversion :: Generation 1 VM. Generation 1 VMs can't use NVMe. Redeploy from a Generation 2 image or convert the Generation 1 VM to Trusted Launch first.

Get the script :: Older versions of the script can hit an HTTP 409 (PropertyChangeNotAllowed) error when Ultra Disk or Premium SSD v2 data disks are attached, because of IOPS/throughput properties in the VM PATCH payload. Always pull the current version as shown (the fix is upstream). This is most relevant for SAP and database workloads, which commonly attach these disk types.
Get the script :: Pull the current version straight from the source repository:
Next steps :: Convert SCSI to NVMe for Linux and Windows VMs
Next steps :: Validate and optimize

Revert the conversion :: If the converted VM doesn't validate, run the script again with -NewControllerType "SCSI" and the original size to switch the controller back. Because the disks are untouched, the revert is a controller and size change, not a restore. Even so, keep the backup from the checklist until validation passes.
Run the conversion :: A typical NVMe conversion, starting the VM afterward and writing a log:
Run the conversion > Parameters that matter :: Parameter | What it does = -FixOperatingSystemSettings | Applies the OS-side changes NVMe needs so the VM boots cleanly on the new interface.

Run the conversion > Parameters that matter :: Parameter | What it does = -IgnoreSKUCheck | Skips the SKU compatibility guardrail. Use only when you know the target is valid and the check is too strict.
Run the conversion > Parameters that matter :: Parameter | What it does = -NewControllerType | Set to NVMe for the move to v6. Set to SCSI to revert a VM if validation fails.
Run the conversion > Parameters that matter :: Parameter | What it does = -StartVM | Starts the VM once the conversion completes, so you can move straight to validation.

Run the conversion > Parameters that matter :: Parameter | What it does = -VMSize | The target size (for example, a _v6 size). The script resizes as part of the conversion. In the example, Standard_D8s_v6 is a non-d (no-temp-disk) size, chosen because the script doesn't support temp-disk source VMs.

Run the conversion > Parameters that matter :: Parameter | What it does = -WriteLogfile | Writes a log of the run. Keep it, it's your record of what changed and your first stop if something looks off.
Set up your session :: Use a process-scoped execution policy so you don't loosen the policy for the whole machine.
Verify the conversion :: Before you hand the VM back, confirm it came up on NVMe. Convert SCSI to NVMe for Linux and Windows VMs walks through the full set of checks. The essentials:

Verify the conversion :: Check that the OS now sees the disks over NVMe. On Linux, list namespaces with lsblk or nvme list and confirm the OS disk is /dev/nvme0n1. On Windows, confirm the disks are healthy in Disk Management under the built-in NVMe controller.
Verify the conversion :: Confirm the target series presents NVMe disks. The Azure Boost availability table lists which sizes do.
Verify the conversion :: If a check fails, revert with the script (see Revert the conversion) and retry after fixing the OS image.
Verify the conversion :: Make sure mounts use stable identifiers, /dev/disk/azure/* symlinks or UUIDs in /etc/fstab, because NVMe device numbers aren't stable across reboots.

managed-identities.name: Managed identities for Azure resources
facts: (top) :: A common challenge for developers is the management of secrets, credentials, certificates, and keys used to secure communication between services. Manual handling of secrets and certificates are a known source of security issues and outages. Managed identities eliminate the need for developers to manage these credentials. Applications can use managed identities to obtain Microsoft Entra tokens without having to manage any credentials.

Azure services that support managed identities :: Managed identities for Azure resources can be used to authenticate to services that support Microsoft Entra authentication. For a list of supported Azure services, see services that support managed identities for Azure resources.

Differences between system-assigned and user-assigned managed identities :: Property | System-assigned managed identity | User-assigned managed identity = Common use cases | Workloads contained within a single Azure resource. Workloads needing independent identities. For example, an application that runs on a single virtual machine. | Workloads that run on multiple resources and can share a single identity. Workloads needing preauthorization to a secure resource, as part of a provisioning flow. Workloads where resources are recycled frequently, but permissions should stay consistent. For example, a workload where multiple virtual machines need to access the same resource.

Differences between system-assigned and user-assigned managed identities :: Property | System-assigned managed identity | User-assigned managed identity = Creation | Created as part of an Azure resource (for example, Azure Virtual Machines or Azure App Service). | Created as a stand-alone Azure resource.

Differences between system-assigned and user-assigned managed identities :: Property | System-assigned managed identity | User-assigned managed identity = Life cycle | Shared life cycle with the Azure resource that the managed identity is created with. When the parent resource is deleted, the managed identity is deleted as well. | Independent life cycle. Must be explicitly deleted.

Differences between system-assigned and user-assigned managed identities :: Property | System-assigned managed identity | User-assigned managed identity = Sharing across Azure resources | Can’t be shared. It can only be associated with a single Azure resource. | Can be shared. The same user-assigned managed identity can be associated with more than one Azure resource.

Use managed identities for Azure resources > Use managed identity as a Federated Identity Credential (FIC) on an Entra ID app :: A workload acting in the capacity of Entra ID application can be hosted on any Azure compute which has a managed identity. The workload uses the managed identity to acquire a token to be exchanged for an Entra ID Application token, via workload identity federation. This feature is also referred to as managed identity as FIC (Federated Identity Credentials). For more information, see configure an application to trust a managed identity.

Use managed identities for Azure resources > Use managed identity as a Federated Identity Credential (FIC) on an Entra ID app :: Workload Identity Federation enables using a managed identity as a credential, just like certificate or password, on Entra ID Applications. Whenever an Entra ID app is required, this is the recommended way to be credential-free. There's a limit of 20 FICs when using managed identities as FIC on an Entra ID App.
Use managed identities for Azure resources > Use managed identity directly :: Authorize the managed identity to have access to the "target" service.

Use managed identities for Azure resources > Use managed identity directly :: Create a managed identity in Azure. You can choose between system-assigned managed identity or user-assigned managed identity.

Use managed identities for Azure resources > Use managed identity directly :: For example, you can use an Azure Virtual Machine (VM) as Azure Compute. You can then create a user-assigned managed identity and assign it to the VM. The workload running on the VM interfaces with both Azure.Identity (or MSAL) and Azure Storage client SDKs to access a storage account. The user-assigned managed identity is authorized to access the storage account.

Use managed identities for Azure resources > Use managed identity directly :: Service code running on your Azure compute resource uses either the Microsoft Authentication Library (MSAL) or Azure.Identity SDK to retrieve a managed identity token from Entra ID backed by the managed identity. This token acquisition doesn't require any secrets and is automatically authenticated based on the environment where the code runs. As long as the managed identity is authorized, the service code can access downstream dependencies that support Entra ID authentication.
Use managed identities for Azure resources > Use managed identity directly :: Typically, you use managed identities in the following steps:

Use managed identities for Azure resources > Use managed identity directly :: Use the managed identity to access a resource. In this step, you can use the Azure SDK with the Azure.Identity library or the Microsoft Authentication Library (MSAL). Some "source" resources offer connectors that know how to use Managed identities for the connections. In that case, you use the identity as a feature of that "source" resource.

Use managed identities for Azure resources > Use managed identity directly :: When using a user-assigned managed identity, you assign the managed identity to the "source" Azure Resource, such as a Virtual Machine, Azure Logic App or an Azure Web App.

What are managed identities? :: A managed identity is an identity that can be assigned to an Azure compute resource (Azure Virtual Machine, Azure Virtual Machine Scale Set, Service Fabric Cluster, Azure Kubernetes cluster) or any App hosting platform supported by Azure. Once a managed identity is assigned on the compute resource, it can be authorized, directly or indirectly, to access downstream dependency resources, such as a storage account, SQL database, Cosmos DB, and so on. Managed identity replaces secrets such as access keys or passwords. In addition, managed identities can replace certificates or other forms of authentication for service-to-service dependencies.

What are managed identities? :: At a high level, there are two types of identities: human and machine/non-human identities. Machine / non-human identities consist of device and workload identities. In Microsoft Entra, workload identities are applications, service principals, and managed identities.

What are managed identities? :: You can use managed identities to authenticate to any resource that supports Microsoft Entra authentication, including your own applications.
What are managed identities? :: You don't need to manage credentials. Credentials aren’t even accessible to you.

resize-vm.name: Resize a virtual machine
facts: (top) :: After you create a VM, you can scale it up or down by changing the VM size. This process works whether the VM is currently running or has already been deallocated.
(top) :: Applies to: ✔️ Linux VMs ✔️ Windows VMs ✔️ Flexible scale sets
(top) :: Deallocating the VM also releases any dynamic IP addresses assigned to the VM. The OS and data disks are not affected.

(top) :: If a resize operation fails, the VM model will still display the requested size, but the VM will continue running on its previous size until the resize is successfully allocated. This behavior applies to both the Azure portal, and all GET operations, as the displayed size always reflects the latest applied configuration, not the actual running size.
(top) :: If the virtual machine is currently running, changing its size will cause it to restart.

(top) :: In some cases, you must deallocate the VM before resizing. Deallocation may be required if the new size isn’t available on the hardware cluster currently hosting the VM. Even when deallocation isn’t required, changing the size of a running VM will cause it to restart. For this reason, resizing a VM should be considered a disruptive operation, especially for stateful workloads.
(top) :: This article shows you how to change an existing virtual machine's VM size.

dsv6.name: Dsv6 series
facts: (top) :: Dsv6-series virtual machines don't have any temporary storage thus lowering the price of entry. You can attach Standard SSDs, Standard HDDs, Premium SSDs, and Premium SSD v2 storage to these virtual machines. You can also attach Ultra Disk storage based on its regional availability. Disk storage is billed separately from virtual machines.

(top) :: Dsv6-series virtual machines run on the 5th Generation Intel® Xeon® Platinum 8573C (Emerald Rapids) processor reaching an all-core turbo clock speed of 3.0 GHz. This new processor features Intel® Turbo Boost Technology, Intel® Advanced-Vector Extensions 512 (Intel® AVX-512), and Intel® Advanced Matrix Extensions. These virtual machines offer up to 192 vCPU and 768 GiB of RAM. Dsv6-series virtual machines provide a better performance for most general-purpose workloads compared to the prior generation (for example, increased scalability, upgraded CPU, elevated memory bandwidth, faster remote storage access).

esv6.name: Esv6 series
facts: (top) :: Esv6-series virtual machines run on the 5th Generation Intel® Xeon® Platinum 8573C (Emerald Rapids) processor reaching an all-core turbo clock speed of 3.0 GHz. This new processor features Intel® Turbo Boost Technology, Intel® Advanced-Vector Extensions 512 (Intel® AVX-512), and Intel® Advanced Matrix Extensions. These virtual machines offer up to 128 vCPU and 1,024 GiB of RAM. Esv6-series virtual machines are ideal for memory-intensive workloads, such as relational database servers, large databases, data analytics engines, in-memory caches, and more.

gen1-trusted-launch.name: Upgrade Gen1 VMs to Trusted launch
facts: (top) :: Applies to: ✔️ Linux VM ✔️ Windows VM ✔️ Generation 1 VM
(top) :: Azure Virtual Machines supports upgrading Generation 1 virtual machines (VM) to Generation 2 by upgrading to the Trusted launch security type.

(top) :: This upgrade path doesn't change the VM CPU architecture. To use Arm64 with Trusted launch, create a new VM from an Arm64 Trusted launch image in Azure Marketplace on supported Cobalt 100 sizes .

(top) :: Trusted launch is a way to enable foundational compute security on Azure Generation 2 VMs and protects against advanced and persistent attack techniques like boot kits and rootkits. It does so by combining infrastructure technologies like Secure Boot, virtual Trusted Platform Module (vTPM), and boot integrity monitoring on your VM.
(top) :: Upgrade of Gen1 VMs to Gen2 without enabling Trusted launch is not supported.
Best practices :: For Linux VMs, validate secure boot compatibility using SBInfo tool. Refer to Linux Trusted launch secure boot validation for distribution-based SBInfo installation commands.
Best practices :: Review known issues and roll-back steps before executing Trusted launch upgrade.

Best practices :: Take full backup OR Create restore points for Azure VMs associated with production workloads before you enable the Trusted launch security type. You can use the backup OR restore points to re-create the disks and VM with the previous Gen1 configuration well-known state.
Best practices :: VM once upgraded to Trusted launch can't be rolled back to Gen1 configuration. It has to be fully recovered using Backup taken before upgrade.

Best practices :: Windows OS disk volume should be defragmented using command Defrag C: /U /V. Defragmentation of OS volume reduces the risk of MBR (Master boot record) to GPT (GUID partition table) conversion failure by freeing up end of partitions. Refer to defrag.

Best practices :: You won't be able to extend Windows OS disk system volume after MBR to GPT conversion as part of upgrade. Recommendation is to extend system volume for future before upgrading to Trusted launch.

Frequently asked questions :: For a Generation 1 VM that doesn't meet the prerequisites to upgrade to Trusted launch, look how to fulfill the prerequisites. For example, If using a virtual machine size not supported, look for an equivalent Trusted launch supported size that supports Trusted launch.

Frequently asked questions :: Trusted launch enables foundational compute security on Azure Generation 2 VMs with no extra cost associated. Also, Trusted launch VMs are majorly on parity with Generation 2 VMs. Hence, there's no added benefit for upgrading only to Generation 2 VM without enabling Trusted launch.
Frequently asked questions :: What if there is Generation 1 VMs, that doesn't fit the prerequisites for Trusted launch?
Frequently asked questions :: Why is upgrade to Generation 2 only (without Trusted launch) not supported?
Known issues > VM image reference doesn't change post Trusted launch upgrade :: Guest patching: For Server OS, Automatic guest patching installs updates based on the image reference of VM.

Known issues > VM image reference doesn't change post Trusted launch upgrade :: Post upgrade of Azure Gen1 VM to Trusted launch, the image reference still reflects source as Gen1 OS image. Image reference not updated is a known limitation.
Known issues > VM image reference doesn't change post Trusted launch upgrade :: Reimage: Reimaging VM using Gen1 image reference post Trusted launch upgrade causes VM boot failure.

Known issues > VM image reference doesn't change post Trusted launch upgrade :: This limitation doesn't impacts the VM or hosted application functionality post Trusted launch upgrade. Following VM operations are impacted due to disconnect between image reference and running OS:
Known issues > Windows 11 boot fails after Trusted launch upgrade of Windows 10 VM :: Resolution: This issue is fixed with 24H2 build version 26100.2314 and 23H2 build version 22631.5624.

Known issues > Windows 11 boot fails after Trusted launch upgrade of Windows 10 VM :: The upgrade can fail if you use outdated Windows 11 installation media. To avoid this issue, ensure you use the most recent Windows 11 image. You can download the latest ISO from the Microsoft Software Download page. If you have a volume licensing agreement, use the Microsoft 365 admin center to access updated Windows 11 images.

Known issues > Windows 11 boot fails after Trusted launch upgrade of Windows 10 VM :: Windows 10 Gen1 VM is successfully upgraded to Trusted launch followed by successful Windows 11 in-place upgrade. However, the Windows 11 boot fails after Azure VM is stopped and started with error shown.

Known issues > Windows Server 2022 boot fails after in-place upgrade of Trusted launch VM migrated from Gen1 :: Windows Server 2019 Gen1 VMs upgraded to Trusted launch followed by an in-place upgrade to Windows Server 2022 might fail to boot with "The boot loader did not load an operating system". This issue is due to partition number mismatch in the UEFI boot entry after MBR-to-GPT conversion. The issue is fixed in Windows Server 2025 and later. Take a snapshot of the OS disk before performing the in-place upgrade.
Known issues > [Windows] D Drive assigned to System Reserved Post upgrade :: After the upgrade check the disks on the server, if system reserved partition has the letter D, do the following actions:
Known issues > [Windows] D Drive assigned to System Reserved Post upgrade :: Reboot the VM
Known issues > [Windows] D Drive assigned to System Reserved Post upgrade :: Reboot the VM to show the temporary storage disk with D: letter
Known issues > [Windows] D Drive assigned to System Reserved Post upgrade :: Reconfigure pagefile from D: to C:
Known issues > [Windows] D Drive assigned to System Reserved Post upgrade :: Remove letter D: from the partition

Known issues > [Windows] D Drive assigned to System Reserved Post upgrade :: Temporary storage Drive letter assignment 'D' is changed to 'E' with previous letter assigned to System Reserved post-upgrade of Gen1 VM. Execute below steps manually post-upgrade to work around the issue:

Known issues > [Windows] MBR to GPT conversion fails with error Cannot find room for the EFI system partition :: Optimize Drives service isn't running or unable to communicate successfully. Service startup type should be set to Manual.

Known issues > [Windows] MBR to GPT conversion fails with error Cannot find room for the EFI system partition :: Run PowerShell cmdlet Get-Partition -DiskNumber 0 to identify current partitions that are configured.

Known issues > [Windows] MBR to GPT conversion fails with error Cannot find room for the EFI system partition :: Run PowerShell cmdlet Remove-Partition -DiskNumber 0 -PartitionNumber X to remove any extra Recovery partition not actively used by Recovery service as identified in Step 1.

Known issues > [Windows] MBR to GPT conversion fails with error Cannot find room for the EFI system partition :: Run ReAgentc /info to identify partition actively used by Recovery. Example: Windows RE location: \\?\GLOBALROOT\device\harddisk0\partition4\Recovery\WindowsRE

Known issues > [Windows] MBR to GPT conversion fails with error Cannot find room for the EFI system partition :: System volume disk is already configured with four MBR partitions (maximum supported by MBR disk layout). You need to delete one of the partitions to make room for EFI system partition.

Known issues > [Windows] MBR to GPT conversion fails with error Cannot find room for the EFI system partition :: System volume is corrupted. You can validate by trying to Shrink Volume by few MBs under Disk Management console. Use command chkdsk C:/v/f to repair system volume.
Known issues > [Windows] MBR to GPT conversion fails with error Cannot find room for the EFI system partition :: There's no free space available on the system volume
Known issues > [Windows] MBR to GPT conversion fails with error Cannot find room for the EFI system partition :: This error occurs for one of following reason:

Known issues > [Windows] MBR to GPT conversion fails with error Cannot find room for the EFI system partition :: Virtual Disk service isn't running or unable to communicate successfully. Service startup type should be set to Manual.
Known issues > [Windows] MBR to GPT failed to update ReAgent.xml :: Complete Gen1 -> Trusted launch upgrade.

Known issues > [Windows] MBR to GPT failed to update ReAgent.xml :: For certain Windows OS versions like Windows 10, MBR2GPT generates pass-through error MBR2GPT: Failed to update ReAgent.xml, please try to manually disable and enable WinRE.
Known issues > [Windows] MBR to GPT failed to update ReAgent.xml :: Open C:\Windows\System32\Recovery\ReAgent.xml and validate BCD GUID in xml file is matching the output from Step 4.

Known issues > [Windows] MBR to GPT failed to update ReAgent.xml :: ReAgent.xml is updated with correct GUID post Windows 11 upgrade, that is, if you don’t take any action between MBR2GPT conversion & Windows 11 upgrade, the GUID value in ReAgent.xml is synced with Windows recovery configuration.
Known issues > [Windows] MBR to GPT failed to update ReAgent.xml :: Run reagentc /disable
Known issues > [Windows] MBR to GPT failed to update ReAgent.xml :: Run reagentc /enable
Known issues > [Windows] MBR to GPT failed to update ReAgent.xml :: Run reagentc /info

Known issues > [Windows] MBR to GPT failed to update ReAgent.xml :: The warning indicates that MBR2GPT.exe was unable to update Recovery partition GUID in C:\Windows\System32\Recovery\ReAgent.xml. This issue shouldn't cause issue with Guest OS functionality or further upgrade operations like Windows 11 Upgrade to succeed or Windows 11 to work properly post Upgrade.

Known issues > [Windows] MBR to GPT failed to update ReAgent.xml :: To manually fix The warning, you can disable and re-enable WinRE post MBR2GPT conversion or post Gen1 to Trusted launch upgrade before Windows 11 upgrade using listed steps, these steps forces sync the WinRE GUID in ReAgent.xml

windows-in-place-upgrade.name: In-place upgrade for VMs running Windows Server in Azure
facts: (top) :: An in-place upgrade allows you to go from an older operating system to a newer one while keeping your settings, server roles, and data intact. This article teaches you how to move your Azure VMs to a later version of Windows Server using an in-place upgrade. Currently, upgrading to Windows Server 2012, Windows Server 2016, Windows Server 2019, Windows Server 2022, and Windows Server 2025 are supported.
(top) :: Azure VM Windows Servicing Stack Reset Tool to reset the Windows Servicing stack.
(top) :: Azure VM Windows Update Error Detection Tool to diagnose specific Windows Update errors
(top) :: Azure Virtual Machine (VM) Windows OS Upgrade Assessment Tool to validate the OS upgrade path and any known issues

(top) :: Following the process in this article causes a disconnection between the data plane and the control plane of the virtual machine (VM). Azure capabilities such as Auto guest patching, Auto OS image upgrades, Hotpatching, and Azure Update Manager are not officially supported and may fail immediately or in the future. This means that the source image information in the VM properties, including the publisher, offer, and plan, remains unchanged. The image used to deploy the VM remains the same, and only the OS is upgraded. To utilize these features, create a new VM using your preferred operating system instead of performing an in-place upgrade.
(top) :: If you're experiencing Windows Update or Windows OS Upgrade issues with virtual machines, before contacting support, run these tools.
(top) :: Trying to diagnose and resolve Windows Update or Windows OS Upgrade issues for your Azure Virtual Machine? Try one of the following tools:
(top) :: Virtual Machine (VM) running in Azure and experiencing Windows Update issues?
Attach upgrade media to the VM :: Attach the upgrade media for the target Windows Server version to the VM which will be upgraded. This can be done while the VM is in the running or stopped state.
Attach upgrade media to the VM > Portal instructions :: In the drop-down for Disk name, select the name of the upgrade disk created in the previous step.
Attach upgrade media to the VM > Portal instructions :: On the Disks page, select Attach existing disks.
Attach upgrade media to the VM > Portal instructions :: On the Virtual machine page, select Disks.
Attach upgrade media to the VM > Portal instructions :: Search for and select Virtual machines.
Attach upgrade media to the VM > Portal instructions :: Select Save to attach the upgrade disk to the VM.
Attach upgrade media to the VM > Portal instructions :: Select a virtual machine to perform the in-place upgrade from the list.
Attach upgrade media to the VM > Portal instructions :: Sign in to the Azure portal.

Create snapshot of the operating system disk :: During the upgrade process, the upgrade media disk is only created in the en-US language. Currently, no other languages or editions are supported. To avoid errors caused by previously using a different language ISO to install the OS, you can set the system language to en-US or change the system locale to English (United States) in Control Panel.

Create snapshot of the operating system disk :: We recommend that you create a snapshot of your operating system disk and any data disks before starting the in-place upgrade process. This enables you to revert to the previous state of the VM if anything fails during the in-place upgrade process. To create a snapshot on each disk, follow these steps to create a snapshot of a disk.
Create upgrade media disk :: If you have more than one subscription, you should run Set-AzContext -Subscription '<subscription name or id> to specify which subscription to use.
Create upgrade media disk :: Parameter | Definition = diskName | Name of the managed disk that will contain the upgrade media
Create upgrade media disk :: Parameter | Definition = location | Azure region where the upgrade media managed disk is created. This must be the same region as the VM to be upgraded.

Create upgrade media disk :: Parameter | Definition = resourceGroup | Name of the resource group where the upgrade media managed disk will be created. The named resource group is created if it doesn't exist.

Create upgrade media disk :: Parameter | Definition = sku | Windows Server upgrade media version. This must be either: server2025Upgrade or server2022Upgrade or server2019Upgrade or server2016Upgrade or server2012Upgrade. The upgrade media disk is created using the latest version of the specified SKU.

Create upgrade media disk :: Parameter | Definition = zone | Azure zone in the selected region where the upgrade media managed disk will be created. This must be the same zone as the VM to be upgraded. For regional VMs (nonzonal) the zone parameter should be "".

Upgrade VM to volume license (KMS server activation) :: The upgrade media provided by Azure requires the VM to be configured for Windows Server volume licensing. This is the default behavior for any Windows Server VM that was installed from a generalized image in Azure. If the VM was imported into Azure, then it might need to be converted to volume licensing to use the upgrade media provided by Azure. To confirm the VM is configured for volume license activation follow these steps to configure the appropriate KMS client setup key. If the activation configuration was changed, then follow these steps to verify connectivity to Azure KMS service.

Upgrade to managed disks :: The in-place upgrade process requires the use of managed disks on the VM to be upgraded. Most VMs in Azure are using managed disks, and retirement for unmanaged disks support was announced in November of 2022. If the VM is currently using unmanaged disks, then follow these steps to migrate to managed disks.
